lessonTitle: Stress Intensity Factor: Characterising the Crack-Tip Field

blocks.text: A 40 mm long crack is found in the skin of an aircraft wing panel carrying 120 MPa. The stress is well below yield, so why does a metallurgist call this a dangerous situation? Because the crack tip, not the average stress, controls whether the panel survives, and one number, the stress intensity factor, captures it.

blocks.markdown: Away from a crack the stress in a loaded plate is roughly the nominal stress $\sigma$ (force divided by area). Close to the tip of a sharp crack the stress is far higher and rises steeply as the tip is approached. What matters is not the exact value at some point, but how strongly the loading and the crack length together drive that tip field. A single scalar, the **stress intensity factor** $K$, measures this strength. Two different cracked bodies with the same $K$ have the same stress field near the tip, so they behave alike in fracture.

blocks.title: Stress intensity factor K
blocks.text: K is the scalar that sets the amplitude of the linear elastic stress field at a crack tip. It depends on the remote stress, the crack size and the body geometry. Its SI unit is $\text{Pa}\sqrt{\text{m}}$, usually quoted as $\text{MPa}\sqrt{\text{m}}$ (note: not MPa).

blocks.caption: Mode I stress intensity factor for a through-thickness crack. $\sigma$ = remote applied stress (MPa), $a$ = crack length parameter (m), $Y$ = dimensionless geometry factor.

blocks.title: K for a central through-crack in a wide plate
blocks.prompt: A wide thin plate carries a remote tensile stress of 120 MPa and contains a central through-thickness crack of total length $2a = 40$ mm. For a crack very small compared with the plate width, $Y = 1$. Find $K$.

steps.text: Identify the crack length parameter. For a central crack, $a$ is the HALF length: $a = 40/2 = 20$ mm $= 0.020$ m.

blocks.markdown: The geometry factor $Y$ absorbs everything that is not $\sigma\sqrt{\pi a}$: where the crack sits, how wide the plate is, and how the load is applied. Typical values are tabulated below (standard handbook values; the secant formula is the common finite-width correction for a central crack of half-length $a$ in a plate of width $W$).

rows: Full crack depth from the edge
blocks.caption: Edge cracks have a larger $Y$ than central cracks of the same $a$ because the free surface lets the crack faces open further.

blocks.title: K for an edge crack
blocks.prompt: A thick flat bar with a single edge crack of depth 8 mm sits under a remote tensile stress of 90 MPa. Use $Y = 1.12$ (wide-plate edge-crack value). Find $K$.

blocks.markdown: **Direction of effects.** Because $K \propto \sigma\sqrt{a}$, doubling the stress doubles $K$, but doubling the crack length raises $K$ only by $\sqrt{2}$. A longer crack at the same stress is always more severe, so cracks that grow make the situation steadily worse.

**Three modes of loading.** Any crack-tip displacement can be split into three independent modes. In **Mode I (opening)** the crack faces separate perpendicular to the crack plane, as under tension normal to the crack. In **Mode II (in-plane shear or sliding)** the faces slide over each other perpendicular to the crack front. In **Mode III (anti-plane shear or tearing)** the faces slide parallel to the crack front, like tearing paper or a torque on a cracked shaft. The corresponding factors are $K_I$, $K_{II}$ and $K_{III}$; most engineering failures are driven by Mode I.

blocks.caption: Opening stress on the crack plane at distance $r$ ahead of a Mode I tip (linear elastic, asymptotic).

blocks.markdown: **Why a stress concentration factor is not enough.** For an elliptical hole of semi-axes $a$ (along the load-normal direction) and $b$, the peak stress is $\sigma_{max} = \sigma(1 + 2a/b)$, a finite multiple of $\sigma$ through the factor $K_t$. As the ellipse flattens into a crack, the tip radius $\rho = b^2/a \to 0$ and $K_t \to \infty$. Equation for $\sigma_{yy}$ above shows the same thing: stress grows like $r^{-1/2}$ and is unbounded as $r\to0$. A single peak-stress number is therefore meaningless for a sharp crack; instead $K$ is the finite quantity that scales the whole singular field.

blocks.title: Real materials do not reach infinity
blocks.text: The singularity is a feature of the linear elastic model. In metals the stress at the tip is capped by yielding in a small plastic zone. LEFM remains valid only while that zone is small compared with the crack length and the remaining ligament.

points: $K = Y\sigma\sqrt{\pi a}$ in $\text{MPa}\sqrt{\text{m}}$; $a$ is the half length for a central crack and the full depth for an edge crack.
Mode I is opening, Mode II is in-plane sliding, Mode III is out-of-plane tearing.
A sharp crack produces a $r^{-1/2}$ stress singularity; $K_t$ diverges as the tip radius tends to zero, so $K$ is used instead.

questions.stem: A cracked bolt is loaded so that the two crack faces slide against each other in the plane of the crack, perpendicular to the crack front. Which loading mode is this?

options.text: Mode I (opening)
Mode III (anti-plane tearing)
A mixed mode that cannot be separated
Mode II (in-plane shear)

distractorRationale.a: Mode I separates the faces rather than sliding them.
distractorRationale.b: Mode III slides faces parallel to the crack front.
distractorRationale.c: Any displacement can be decomposed into the three modes; here only one is present.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: sliding perpendicular to the front within the crack plane is Mode II.

questions.explanation: Sliding of the faces within the plane of the crack and normal to the front is the definition of in-plane shear, Mode II. Opening would separate the faces, and tearing would slide them parallel to the crack front.

questions.stem: A technician says the stress at a sharp crack tip is 'just the stress concentration factor times the nominal stress'. Why is this wrong?

options.text: Stress concentration factors only exist for circular holes
Stress concentration factors apply only to compressive loading
The crack tip stress is always exactly equal to the nominal stress
For a sharp crack the tip radius tends to zero, so the concentration factor becomes unbounded and gives no usable value

questions.correctOptionText: For a sharp crack the tip radius tends to zero, so the concentration factor becomes unbounded and gives no usable value

distractorRationale.a: Factors exist for ellipses, notches, fillets and many shapes, not only circles.
distractorRationale.b: They apply to tension as well; this is not the reason.
distractorRationale.c: The tip stress is much higher than nominal in the elastic model.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: with radius tending to zero the factor diverges, so K is used instead.

questions.explanation: A concentration factor needs a finite peak stress, but for a sharp tip the elastic stress varies as $r^{-1/2}$ and grows without bound as $r\to0$. Hence a different parameter, the stress intensity factor, is needed to scale the whole near-tip field.

questions.stem: A plate has crack A with remote stress $\sigma$ and length $a$. A second identical plate has remote stress $\sigma/2$ and a crack of length $4a$ (same geometry factor). How does $K$ in the second plate compare with the first?

options.text: Equal
Half as large
Twice as large
Four times as large

distractorRationale.b: That forgets the square root on length.
distractorRationale.c: That would need only the length term ($\sqrt4$) without the halved stress.
distractorRationale.d: That treats $K$ as linear in length and ignores the halved stress.

questions.explanation: Since $K\propto\sigma\sqrt{a}$, the ratio is $(1/2)\times\sqrt{4} = 1$. Reducing the stress by half exactly offsets quadrupling the crack length.

questions.stem: A circumferential crack runs around a round shaft that is loaded only in pure torsion. Which mode dominates the crack front, to a good approximation for a shallow crack?

options.text: Mode III
Mode I
Mode II
No mode, because the load is a couple

distractorRationale.a: Correct: torsion makes faces slide parallel to the circumferential crack front.
distractorRationale.b: Mode I needs a tensile stress normal to the crack plane.
distractorRationale.c: Mode II requires sliding perpendicular to the front, not parallel.
distractorRationale.d: Torsional loading does load the crack in shear.

questions.explanation: Torque produces shear stresses along the circumferential direction, which slide the crack faces parallel to the crack front. That is anti-plane shear, Mode III.

questions.stem: Which statement about the units of the stress intensity factor is correct?

options.text: It is expressed in MPa$\sqrt{\text{m}}$ because it is stress multiplied by the square root of length
It is expressed in MPa because it is a stress
It is expressed in N/m because it is an energy per area
It is dimensionless because $Y$ is dimensionless

questions.correctOptionText: It is expressed in MPa$\sqrt{\text{m}}$ because it is stress multiplied by the square root of length

distractorRationale.a: Correct: $\sigma\sqrt{\pi a}$ gives stress times root length.
distractorRationale.b: Plain MPa omits the length dependence.
distractorRationale.c: N/m is the unit of energy release rate, a different quantity.
distractorRationale.d: $Y$ is dimensionless but $\sigma\sqrt{\pi a}$ is not.

questions.explanation: $K = Y\sigma\sqrt{\pi a}$ has the units of stress multiplied by the square root of length, so MPa$\sqrt{\text{m}}$. Energy release rate has units of N/m, which is a related but different quantity.

questions.stem: A single edge crack of depth 3 mm lies in a wide plate under a remote tensile stress of 200 MPa. Taking $Y = 1.12$, compute $K_I$ in MPa$\sqrt{\text{m}}$.
questions.explanation: With $a=0.003$ m, $\sqrt{\pi a}=0.0971$, so $K = 1.12\times200\times0.0971 = 21.7$ MPa$\sqrt{\text{m}}$. The depth must be converted to metres before applying the formula.

questions.stem: A wide plate with a central crack of total length 10 mm is to carry a stress such that $K_I$ must not exceed 20 MPa$\sqrt{\text{m}}$. Taking $Y=1.1$, find the largest allowable remote stress in MPa.
questions.explanation: The half length is $a=0.005$ m, so $\sqrt{\pi a}=0.125$. Rearranging, $\sigma = K/(Y\sqrt{\pi a}) = 20/(1.1\times0.125) = 145$ MPa. Using the full length instead of the half length would give a wrong stress.

questions.stem: A central crack of total length 50 mm lies in a finite plate of width $W = 200$ mm under a remote stress of 100 MPa. Use the secant correction $Y=\sqrt{\sec(\pi a/W)}$ with $a$ the half length. Compute $K_I$ in MPa$\sqrt{\text{m}}$.
questions.explanation: The half length is $a=0.025$ m so $\pi a/W = 0.3927$ rad and $Y=\sqrt{\sec(0.3927)}=1.04$. Then $K = 1.04\times100\times\sqrt{\pi\times0.025} = 29.2$ MPa$\sqrt{\text{m}}$. The finite width raises $K$ about 4 percent above the infinite-plate value.

questions.stem: Explain, using the near-tip stress field, why the peak stress at a sharp crack tip cannot be characterised by a stress concentration factor, and say what quantity is used instead.
markingGuide: States that the elastic tip stress varies as $K/\sqrt{2\pi r}$ and tends to infinity as $r\to0$
Notes that $K_t = 1+2a/b$ (or similar) diverges as the tip radius tends to zero
Says $K$ scales the amplitude of the whole singular field and combines load, crack size and geometry
Mentions that real materials relieve the singularity by local yielding, so LEFM needs a small plastic zone
questions.explanation: A stress concentration factor presumes a finite peak stress that scales with nominal stress. For a sharp crack the elastic field is singular, so the factor is unbounded. The stress intensity factor remains finite and fully describes the field amplitude.

questions.stem: Three cracks are found in separate components: (i) a through-wall crack in a tensile test bar loaded axially, crack plane normal to the load; (ii) a crack in a keyed shaft end loaded purely in torsion with a circumferential crack front; (iii) a crack in a plate loaded in in-plane shear parallel to the crack plane. Classify the dominant mode of each and describe the relative crack-face motion for each.
markingGuide: (i) Mode I, faces separate normal to the crack plane
(ii) Mode III, faces slide parallel to the crack front (anti-plane)
(iii) Mode II, faces slide in the crack plane perpendicular to the front
Mentions that the three modes are independent displacement fields that superpose, each with its own K
questions.explanation: Opening is Mode I, in-plane sliding perpendicular to the front is Mode II, and tearing parallel to the front is Mode III. Any real loading is a combination of these, and each mode has its own stress intensity factor.
